title: Quasar J0100+2802 (NIRCam Image)
caption: The field around quasar J0100+2802, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, S. Lilly (ETH Zurich), D. Kashino (Nagoya University), J. Matthee (ETH Zurich), C. Eilers (MIT), R. Simcoe (MIT), R. Bordoloi (MIT), R. Mackenzie (ETH Zurich), A. Pagan (STScI)

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Webb image archive. No published rating.

story: Thousands of tiny galaxies in varied colours spread across black space, some of the smallest in shades of orange and pink. At the centre sits a small pink object with six diffraction spikes, a little smaller than the blue foreground stars. It is quasar J0100+2802, an active supermassive black hole. The field holds more than 20,000 galaxies and lies between Pisces and Andromeda.

The quasar is so bright that it lights up the gas between it and Webb like a flashlight. The EIGER team studied 117 galaxies from approximately 900 million years after the big bang, concentrating on the 59 in front of the quasar, and the illuminated gas around them.

These galaxies come from shortly before the Era of Reionisation ended. The early Universe's gas cooled over hundreds of millions of years, then became hot, ionised and transparent again. Webb shows galaxies had cleared transparent bubbles around themselves, fully ionising gas within a 2 million light-year radius.

understand.summary: This Webb NIRCam image combines three near-infrared filters. Light at 1.15 μm is shown in blue, 2.0 μm in green and 3.56 μm in red.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and nearly all of these galaxies are far too faint and distant to see without Webb.

explore: That radius is roughly the distance between the Milky Way and Andromeda. In the following hundred million years the bubbles grew and merged, making the whole Universe transparent. The team plans to study six fields, each centred on a quasar, though these first NIRCam images and spectra are already detailed enough for firm conclusions.
